stem: A 58-year-old man who smokes has had 40 minutes of crushing pressure in the centre of his chest that spreads to his left arm and jaw, with sweating and nausea. Rest and a nitroglycerin tablet do not help. The ECG shows ST elevation in V1–V4.
oneliner: 58M smoker + 40 min crushing chest pressure → left arm and jaw + sweating, nausea + no relief with rest or nitroglycerin + ST elevation V1–V4
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Sudden breathlessness + low oxygen + fast heart rate**, usually with a clot risk
whyNot.C: **Sharp pain, better leaning forward + friction rub + ST elevation in almost all leads**
whyNot.D: **Brief, brought on by exertion and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin**; no ST elevation
whyNot.E: **Tearing pain through to the back + blood pressure difference between the arms**

answer: Anterior wall myocardial infarction (left anterior descending artery)
why: **Persistent pain not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin + ST elevation in V1–V4** = anterior ST-elevation MI from the left anterior descending artery.

stem: A 76-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes has had 2 hours of nausea, sweating and sudden breathlessness, but no chest pain. Her pulse is 104/min and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Troponin I is raised and the ECG shows new ST depression in V4–V6.
oneliner: 76F + long-standing diabetes + nausea, sweating, breathlessness, no chest pain + pulse 104, SpO2 96% + troponin raised + new ST depression V4–V6
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Low oxygen + clot risk**; ECG usually only a fast heart rate
whyNot.B: **Normal troponin and ECG**; usually younger with recurrent episodes
whyNot.C: Same ECG picture, but **troponin stays normal**
whyNot.D: **Positional pain + friction rub + widespread ST elevation**

why: **Raised troponin + new ischemic ECG changes** = myocardial infarction. Older women and people with diabetes often have **no chest pain** (autonomic neuropathy).

stem: A 63-year-old man has had 1 hour of heavy chest pain with vomiting. His pulse is 44/min and his blood pressure is 92/60 mm Hg, equal in both arms. The ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF.
oneliner: 63M + 1 h heavy chest pain + vomiting + pulse 44 + BP 92/60, equal in both arms + ST elevation II, III, aVF
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **ST elevation in almost all leads + PR depression**
whyNot.B: **ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6** (circumflex artery)
whyNot.D: **ST elevation in V1–V4** (left anterior descending artery)
whyNot.E: **Tearing pain to the back + arm blood pressure difference**

answer: Inferior wall myocardial infarction (right coronary artery)
why: **ST elevation in II, III and aVF** = inferior wall, usually the right coronary artery. It often supplies the SA and AV nodes, so **slow heart rate** is common.

stem: A 59-year-old man with chest pain has ST elevation in II, III and aVF and in the right-sided lead V4R. After one nitroglycerin tablet his blood pressure falls from 110/70 to 78/50 mm Hg. His neck veins are distended, his lungs are clear with equal breath sounds, and his oxygen saturation is 96% on room air.
oneliner: 59M + chest pain + ST elevation II, III, aVF and V4R + BP falls after nitroglycerin + distended neck veins + clear lungs, equal breath sounds + SpO2 96%
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Muffled heart sounds + pulsus paradoxus**, no regional ST elevation
whyNot.B: **Crackles in the lungs** (pulmonary edema)
whyNot.D: **Low oxygen + fast heart rate + pleuritic pain**
whyNot.E: **Trachea pushed away + absent breath sounds on one side**

why: **ST elevation in V4R + low blood pressure after nitrates + distended neck veins with clear lungs** (with inferior MI) = right ventricular infarct; the right ventricle depends on preload, so nitrates drop the blood pressure.

stem: A 67-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension has sudden, severe tearing chest pain that goes through to his back. Blood pressure is 168/94 mm Hg in the right arm and 128/80 mm Hg in the left. A new soft diastolic murmur is heard at the right sternal border.
oneliner: 67M + poorly controlled hypertension + sudden tearing chest pain → back + arm BP 168/94 vs 128/80 + new diastolic murmur at right sternal border
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Pressure-like pain + ST changes in one territory**; equal arm pressures
whyNot.B: **Abdominal or flank pain + pulsatile abdominal mass + shock**
whyNot.C: **Positional pain + friction rub**
whyNot.D: **Low oxygen + fast heart rate + clot risk**

why: **Tearing pain to the back + blood pressure difference between the arms + new aortic regurgitation murmur** = aortic dissection.

stem: A 24-year-old very tall man with long fingers, who had a dislocated lens as a child, suddenly develops severe tearing chest pain going through to his back while lifting weights. Breath sounds are equal on both sides. A chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum.
oneliner: 24M + very tall, long fingers + childhood lens dislocation + sudden tearing chest pain → back while lifting + equal breath sounds + widened mediastinum
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Mid-systolic click**; usually no pain or collapse
whyNot.B: **Rare at 24 without cocaine**; no widened mediastinum
whyNot.C: **Fainting on exertion + systolic murmur louder with Valsalva**; no tearing pain or widened mediastinum
whyNot.E: Also tall, thin and young, but **absent breath sounds on one side** and a normal mediastinum

why: **Marfan features + tearing pain to the back + widened mediastinum** = dissection from cystic medial degeneration of the aorta.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had 2 days of sharp chest pain that is worse lying flat and on breathing in, and better sitting forward. She had a cold a week ago. Her blood pressure and oxygen saturation are normal. A scratchy three-part sound is heard at the left sternal border. The ECG shows ST elevation in almost every lead with PR depression.
oneliner: 29F + sharp chest pain, worse lying flat, better sitting forward + cold 1 week ago + normal BP and SpO2 + scratchy 3-part sound + ST elevation almost every lead, PR depression
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Pain reproduced by pressing the chest wall**; normal ECG
whyNot.B: **Low oxygen + fast heart rate + clot risk**
whyNot.C: **Low blood pressure + distended neck veins + muffled heart sounds**
whyNot.D: **ST elevation in one coronary territory** with reciprocal changes

why: **Pain better leaning forward + friction rub + ST elevation in almost every lead with PR depression** = acute (often viral) pericarditis.

stem: A 61-year-old man is seen 3 weeks after a large anterior myocardial infarction with fever and sharp chest pain that eases when he leans forward. His blood pressure and oxygen saturation are normal. A scratchy three-part sound is heard at the left sternal border. The ECG shows ST elevation in almost every lead and troponin is normal.
oneliner: 61M + 3 weeks after anterior MI + fever + sharp chest pain, eases leaning forward + normal BP and SpO2 + scratchy 3-part sound + ST elevation almost every lead, normal troponin
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **New ST elevation in one territory + rising troponin**, pressure-like pain
whyNot.B: **Low oxygen + fast heart rate**
whyNot.D: **5–14 days after MI: sudden tamponade and collapse**
whyNot.E: **2–7 days after MI: new holosystolic murmur + pulmonary edema**

why: **Weeks after an MI + fever + pain better leaning forward + friction rub** = Dressler syndrome, an autoimmune pericarditis.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer has had 3 days of worsening breathlessness. Her blood pressure is 86/60 mm Hg, pulse 120/min and oxygen saturation 95%; the systolic pressure falls by 14 mm Hg when she breathes in. Her neck veins are distended, her heart sounds are muffled and her lungs are clear with equal breath sounds.
oneliner: 54F + metastatic lung cancer + 3 days worsening breathlessness + BP 86/60, pulse 120, SpO2 95% + systolic falls 14 on breathing in + distended neck veins + muffled heart sounds + clear lungs, equal breath sounds
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Slow onset over months + Kussmaul sign + pericardial knock**
whyNot.C: **Low oxygen + clear heart sounds**
whyNot.D: **Swollen face and arms + dilated chest veins**, normal blood pressure
whyNot.E: **Trachea pushed away + absent breath sounds on one side**

why: **Low blood pressure + distended neck veins + muffled heart sounds (Beck triad) + pulsus paradoxus** = tamponade, here from a malignant effusion.

stem: A 17-year-old girl has had 3 days of sharp left-sided chest pain since starting rowing practice. Pressing on the junction of her ribs and breastbone reproduces the pain exactly. Her vital signs, ECG and chest x-ray are normal.
oneliner: 17F + 3 days sharp left chest pain after starting rowing + pain reproduced by pressing rib-breastbone junction + normal vitals, ECG, x-ray
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Low oxygen + fast heart rate**
whyNot.C: **ST changes + raised troponin**; pain not reproduced by pressure
whyNot.D: **Friction rub + ST elevation in almost every lead**
whyNot.E: **Absent breath sounds on one side**

why: **Pain reproduced exactly by pressing the rib–breastbone junction + normal tests** = costochondritis.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who smokes wakes at about 5 a.m. several times a week with chest pain lasting 10 minutes. During one episode the ECG shows ST elevation that disappears completely afterwards. Troponin stays normal and coronary angiography is normal.
oneliner: 34F smoker + early-morning chest pain at rest, 10 min + transient ST elevation + normal troponin + normal coronary angiography
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Pain on exertion + ST depression**
whyNot.C: **ST elevation in almost every lead for days + friction rub**
whyNot.D: **Troponin rises**
whyNot.E: **Rest pain from a plaque + ST depression**, abnormal angiogram

why: **Pain at rest in the early morning + ST elevation that comes and goes + normal coronary arteries** = coronary artery spasm.

stem: A 61-year-old man gets chest tightness when he walks uphill; it lasts 3–4 minutes and eases within minutes of resting. His resting ECG is normal, and an exercise test brings on ST depression in V4–V6.
oneliner: 61M + chest tightness walking uphill, 3–4 min, eases with rest + normal resting ECG + ST depression V4–V6 on exercise
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Pain at rest or getting worse quickly**
whyNot.B: **Prolonged pain + troponin rise**
whyNot.D: **Pain reproduced by pressing the chest wall**
whyNot.E: **Pain at rest in the early morning + ST elevation**

why: **Predictable pain on exertion, relieved by rest + ST depression on exercise** = stable angina from a fixed narrowing (usually over 70%).

stem: A 57-year-old man with known exertional angina now has chest pain at rest lasting 20 minutes, three times in the past day. The ECG shows ST depression in V4–V6, and troponin is normal on two checks.
oneliner: 57M + known exertional angina + rest chest pain 20 min, 3 times in a day + ST depression V4–V6 + troponin normal twice
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Early-morning rest pain + transient ST elevation + normal coronaries**
whyNot.B: **Positional pain + friction rub**
whyNot.C: **Only on exertion, relieved by rest**
whyNot.E: Same picture but **troponin rises**

why: **New pain at rest or a worsening pattern + ST depression + normal troponin** = unstable angina.

stem: A 3-day-old boy with a 22q11.2 deletion has cyanosis and fast breathing. Echocardiography shows a single great vessel leaving the heart above a ventricular septal defect.
oneliner: 3d M + 22q11.2 deletion + cyanosis + echo: single great vessel over a VSD → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Two separate great vessels, aorta from the right ventricle**; here only one vessel leaves the heart
whyNot.B: **Separate aortic and pulmonary outlets with pulmonary stenosis**; here there is one common trunk
whyNot.D: **Normal two great vessels** with abnormal pulmonary vein drainage; here a single trunk
whyNot.E: **No tricuspid valve and a small right ventricle**; the echo finding here is a single trunk over a VSD

answer: Persistent truncus arteriosus (failure of aorticopulmonary septum formation)
why: **A single great vessel over a VSD** with 22q11.2 deletion = failed neural crest-driven outflow tract septation = truncus arteriosus.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash with an open femur fracture and heavy bleeding. Pulse is 122/min, BP 96/68 mm Hg, and respirations 24/min. His skin is cool and pale, his neck veins are flat, and breath sounds are equal and clear.
oneliner: 28M + open femur fracture with heavy bleeding + HR 122 + BP 96/68 + cool pale skin + flat neck veins → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Cool pale skin with tachycardia**; neurogenic shock gives warm skin and bradycardia
whyNot.B: **Flat neck veins and clear lungs**; pump failure would give venous congestion
whyNot.C: **Equal, clear breath sounds and flat neck veins**; distended veins and absent breath sounds would be expected
whyNot.E: **Visible blood loss and cool skin**; septic shock gives warm flushed skin and fever

why: **Major bleeding + tachycardia + cool skin + flat neck veins** = volume loss with compensatory vasoconstriction.

stem: A 57-year-old man with heavy alcohol use vomits bright red blood twice. Pulse is 125/min and BP is 85/45 mm Hg. His skin is cool and clammy. He has no fever, rash, or wheeze, and his neck veins are flat.
oneliner: 57M + hematemesis + HR 125 + BP 85/45 + cool clammy skin + flat neck veins → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Flat neck veins**; congestion would raise them
whyNot.C: **Afebrile with cool skin and an obvious blood source**; sepsis gives fever and warm skin early
whyNot.D: **No rash or wheeze** and no allergen exposure
whyNot.E: **Cool clammy skin with tachycardia**; neurogenic shock gives warm skin and bradycardia

why: **Hematemesis with tachycardia, hypotension, and cool clammy skin** = hypovolemia from GI blood loss.

stem: A 31-year-old man is brought in after a stab wound to the left flank. Pulse is 130/min and BP is 54/48 mm Hg. His skin is cool and mottled, his abdomen is distended, his neck veins are flat, and heart sounds are normal.
oneliner: 31M + flank stab wound + HR 130 + BP 54/48 + mottled skin + flat neck veins + normal heart sounds → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Flat neck veins and normal heart sounds**; tamponade gives distended veins and muffled sounds
whyNot.B: **Penetrating trauma with cool mottled skin and a tiny pulse pressure**; sepsis gives a wide pulse pressure
whyNot.C: **Tachycardia and cool skin**; neurogenic shock has bradycardia and warm skin
whyNot.E: **Flat neck veins**; tension pneumothorax gives distended veins, and the wound here is in the flank

why: **Penetrating abdominal injury, tachycardia, pulse pressure of only 6 mm Hg, flat veins** = massive blood loss.

stem: A 40-year-old woman arrives after a deep calf laceration with heavy bleeding. Pulse is 118/min and BP is 90/70 mm Hg. Her skin is cool and capillary refill is slow. Pulmonary artery catheter readings: cardiac output 3.0 L/min (normal 4–8), central venous pressure 1 mm Hg (normal 2–8), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 3 mm Hg (normal 6–12), systemic vascular resistance 2,000 dyne·s/cm⁵ (normal 800–1,200).
oneliner: 40F + calf laceration bleeding + HR 118 + BP 90/70 + CO 3.0 + CVP 1 + wedge 3 + SVR 2,000 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **High cardiac output and low vascular resistance**; here output is low and resistance high
whyNot.C: **High wedge pressure and high CVP**; here both are low
whyNot.D: **Low vascular resistance**; here resistance is high
whyNot.E: **High, equalized CVP and wedge pressures**; here both are low

why: **Low CO, low CVP and wedge, high SVR** after bleeding = loss of preload with compensatory vasoconstriction.

stem: A 64-year-old man has 2 hours of crushing chest pain with sweating. ECG shows ST elevation in V1–V4. Pulse is 112/min and BP is 82/68 mm Hg. His skin is cool and clammy, his jugular venous pressure is raised, and he has fine crackles at both bases. The trachea is midline and BP is the same in both arms.
oneliner: 64M + crushing chest pain + ST elevation V1–V4 + BP 82/68 + HR 112 + raised JVP + basal crackles → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Raised JVP and crackles**; blood loss gives flat veins and clear lungs
whyNot.C: **Midline trachea and bibasal crackles**; hyperresonance and tracheal shift are absent
whyNot.D: **Equal arm pressures and ST elevation with crackles**; no tearing pain or pressure differential
whyNot.E: **Cool clammy skin with raised JVP and crackles, no fever**; sepsis gives warm skin and flat veins

why: **Anterior STEMI + hypotension with a narrow pulse pressure + raised JVP and crackles** = pump failure.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has sudden left flank pain and blood in her urine. She is afebrile and urinalysis shows no white cells. Her pulse is irregularly irregular and ECG shows no P waves. CT of the abdomen shows wedge-shaped hypodense areas in the left kidney.
oneliner: 72F + sudden flank pain + hematuria + afebrile + irregularly irregular pulse + wedge-shaped renal hypodensities on CT → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of the CT finding?

whyNot.A: **Wedge-shaped infarcts with sudden pain**; stenosis causes chronic hypertension and a small kidney
whyNot.B: **No fever and no pyuria**
whyNot.C: **Wedge-shaped hypodensities, not a solid mass**, with an acute onset
whyNot.E: **Arterial wedge infarcts and an irregular rhythm** point to emboli; vein thrombosis causes a swollen kidney with nephrotic features

why: **Irregularly irregular pulse with no P waves + wedge-shaped renal infarcts** = AF throwing atrial emboli.

stem: A 52-year-old man has 2 hours of palpitations and light-headedness. ECG shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 138/min with no distinct P waves.
oneliner: 52M + palpitations 2 h + light-headed + ECG irregularly irregular + no P waves → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Irregular rhythm with no sawtooth waves**; flutter is usually regular
whyNot.B: **Irregularly irregular** rather than regular
whyNot.C: **No P waves at all**, rather than three or more P-wave shapes
whyNot.D: **No P waves** and an irregular rhythm

why: **Irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no P waves** = atrial fibrillation.

stem: A 68-year-old man has an irregularly irregular pulse of 72/min at rest with no P waves on ECG. When he climbs stairs his rate rises to 150/min and he becomes short of breath.
oneliner: 68M + irregularly irregular pulse 72 at rest + no P waves + HR 150 and dyspnea on stairs → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No P waves**, and no lung disease is described
whyNot.B: **Irregular with no flutter waves**; flutter is usually regular
whyNot.C: **Irregular and graded with exercise**, not abrupt and regular
whyNot.D: **No P waves** at rest and irregular pulse

why: **Irregularly irregular pulse with absent P waves** = atrial fibrillation; the exertional rise reflects sympathetic drive on AV conduction.

stem: A 45-year-old woman, one day after cholecystectomy, suddenly develops palpitations. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190/min with no visible P waves. BP is 118/74 mm Hg.
oneliner: 45F + post-op day 1 + sudden palpitations + regular narrow-complex tachycardia 190 + no P waves → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Regular rhythm**, not irregularly irregular
whyNot.B: **Rate 190 and no flutter waves**; 2:1 flutter runs near 150/min
whyNot.C: **Abrupt onset at 190/min**, above the usual sinus maximum, and no P waves
whyNot.E: **Narrow QRS**

why: **Abrupt onset, regular narrow-complex rhythm at 190/min without P waves** = reentrant SVT.

stem: A 62-year-old man, 3 days after an anterior MI, has sudden palpitations and light-headedness. BP is 104/70 mm Hg. ECG shows a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 170/min with a QRS of 0.16 s; P waves march through independent of the QRS.
oneliner: 62M + 3 d post anterior MI + palpitations + regular wide-complex tachycardia 170 + QRS 0.16 s + P waves independent of QRS → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Atrial fibrillation with a bundle branch block

whyNot.A: **Wide QRS with AV dissociation**; flutter shows flutter waves and a fixed ratio
whyNot.B: **P waves dissociated from the QRS**, which does not occur in SVT
whyNot.C: **Regular rhythm** rather than irregularly irregular
whyNot.D: **Uniform QRS complexes**, not twisting around the baseline

why: **Wide regular tachycardia with AV dissociation after MI** = ventricular tachycardia from ischemic scar or border zone.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who drinks 8 cups of coffee daily has had skipped beats for several weeks. Pulse is 78/min and BP is normal. A rhythm strip shows regular sinus beats with occasional early narrow-complex beats, each preceded by a P wave of a different shape.
oneliner: 29F + 8 cups coffee/day + weeks of palpitations + strip: occasional early narrow beats with abnormal P wave → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Mostly regular sinus rhythm with only occasional early beats**, and P waves are present
whyNot.C: **Rate 78/min**, not tachycardic
whyNot.D: **Narrow QRS preceded by a P wave**; PVCs are wide with no P wave
whyNot.E: **No pauses or sustained bradycardia**; the rate is 78/min

why: **Early narrow-complex beats with an abnormal P wave** = premature atrial contractions, often provoked by caffeine.

stem: A 35-year-old man has occasional skipped beats. A rhythm strip shows regular sinus beats, with a single early wide, bizarre QRS (0.14 s) that has no preceding P wave, followed by a pause before the next normal beat. Echocardiography is normal.
oneliner: 35M + skipped beats + strip: single early wide QRS, no P wave, then a pause → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No premature P wave before the wide beat**
whyNot.B: **Only one abnormal beat**, not three or more in a row
whyNot.C: **Early rather than late in the cycle**; escape beats follow a long pause
whyNot.E: **The wide beat comes early**; escape beats appear after a prolonged pause

why: **Single early wide QRS with no P wave and a pause** = premature ventricular contraction.

stem: A 72-year-old man faints at rest. His pulse is a regular 40/min, with intermittent cannon a waves in the neck. ECG shows P waves at 85/min that bear no relation to the QRS complexes.
oneliner: 72M + syncope + regular pulse 40 + cannon a waves + P waves unrelated to QRS → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II

whyNot.A: **P waves unrelated to the QRS**; Mobitz II has a fixed PR with dropped beats
whyNot.B: **P waves are not conducted at all**; first-degree block only lengthens a constant PR, and every P is followed by a QRS
whyNot.C: **Normal sinus P waves at 85/min**; the problem is conduction below the atria
whyNot.D: **Atrial rate 85 with ventricular rate 40**, so the P waves and QRS are dissociated

why: **P waves unrelated to QRS + regular slow ventricular rate + cannon a waves** = complete AV dissociation.

stem: A 78-year-old woman who recently started propranolol faints while standing at the stove. Pulse is 45/min and regular. ECG shows a P wave before every QRS with a constant PR interval of 0.18 s. Monitoring shows no pauses. Symptoms stop when the dose is halved.
oneliner: 78F + new propranolol + syncope + pulse 45 + P before every QRS + constant PR + resolves with dose cut → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No pauses and a clear drug trigger that reverses**
whyNot.B: **Every P wave is followed by a QRS** at a constant PR interval
whyNot.C: **Persistent slow pulse with no emotional or postural trigger**
whyNot.D: **Constant PR with no dropped beats**

why: **Normal P-QRS relationship at 45/min that resolves when the beta blocker is reduced** = drug-induced sinus bradycardia.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has fainted twice while swimming. Her uncle died suddenly at age 25. Coronary angiography and echocardiography are normal. ECG shows a corrected QT of 510 ms, a normal PR interval, no delta wave, and normal ST segments in V1–V3.
oneliner: 19F + syncope while swimming ×2 + uncle with sudden death + normal coronaries and echo + QTc 510 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Long QT with normal V1–V3 ST segments**; Brugada has coved ST elevation in V1–V3
whyNot.C: **Normal echocardiogram**
whyNot.D: **Normal PR and no delta wave**
whyNot.E: **Prolonged resting QT**; the resting ECG in CPVT is normal

why: **Syncope with a family sudden death, structurally normal heart, and QTc 510 ms** = congenital long QT syndrome.

stem: A 7-year-old boy with congenital bilateral sensorineural deafness has fainting spells during play. ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. His parents hear normally and have normal ECGs; his vision and urinalysis are normal.
oneliner: 7M + congenital deafness + fainting during play + long QT + hearing parents with normal ECGs → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Deafness is present**; Romano-Ward has normal hearing and is dominant
whyNot.B: **Prolonged QT**, not coved ST elevation in V1–V3, and no deafness
whyNot.D: **Normal vision**; Usher pairs deafness with retinitis pigmentosa and a normal QT
whyNot.E: **Normal urinalysis**; Alport pairs deafness with hematuria and has a normal QT

why: **Congenital deafness + long QT + syncope with unaffected parents** = autosomal recessive potassium channel defect.

stem: A 66-year-old man started hydrochlorothiazide 2 weeks ago and now feels dizzy when he stands from bed. Supine: BP 128/80 mm Hg, pulse 74/min. After 3 minutes standing: BP 104/66 mm Hg, pulse 96/min. Serum sodium is 133 mEq/L and BUN is 28 mg/dL (normal 7–20). He has no headaches or sweating spells.
oneliner: 66M + new HCTZ + dizzy on standing + BP 128/80 → 104/66 + pulse 74 → 96 + Na 133 + BUN 28 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Dizziness occurs reliably on standing with a BP fall at 3 min**, not after a trigger like pain or fear
whyNot.B: **Heart rate rises by 22/min**; in autonomic failure it stays fixed
whyNot.C: **No headaches or sweating spells and normal supine BP**
whyNot.E: **Standing BP drop, not a neck-pressure trigger**

why: **BP fall with a compensatory pulse rise on standing after starting a thiazide** = volume-depletion orthostatic hypotension.

stem: An 88-year-old man with long-standing hypertension faints when the examiner presses on the right side of his neck. The monitor shows a 4-second sinus pause at that moment; his baseline ECG is normal.
oneliner: 88M + faints when neck is pressed + 4 s pause on monitor + normal baseline ECG → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Faint triggered by neck pressure**, not by standing, pain, or emotion
whyNot.C: **Normal baseline ECG** with pauses only on neck pressure
whyNot.D: **Pause (asystole) rather than a fast rhythm**
whyNot.E: **Syncope occurs with neck pressure**, not on standing

why: **Syncope with a sinus pause on neck pressure in an older man** = exaggerated carotid baroreflex.

stem: A 33-year-old woman collapses 1 minute after finishing a marathon. She recovers fully within a minute of lying flat, with no convulsions, tongue biting, or confusion. ECG, echocardiogram, and resting orthostatic vitals are normal.
oneliner: 33F + collapses 1 min after finishing marathon + recovers on lying flat + no seizure features + normal ECG and echo → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal ECG and collapse only after stopping**; arrhythmic syncope occurs during exertion
whyNot.C: **Normal resting orthostatic vitals**
whyNot.D: **No convulsions, tongue biting, or postictal confusion**
whyNot.E: **Normal echocardiogram**

why: **Collapse just after stopping vigorous exercise with rapid recovery lying down and a normal heart** = loss of the muscle pump drops venous return.

stem: A 58-year-old man who smokes has had exertional breathlessness for 3 months without chest pain. His father had an MI at 52. Chest is clear, there is no murmur, and resting echo shows normal wall thickness. At peak stress echo there is new hypokinesis of the inferior wall that resolves at rest.
oneliner: 58M + smoker + exertional dyspnea + father MI at 52 + clear chest, no murmur, normal wall thickness + new inferior hypokinesis at peak stress → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Normal wall thickness on echo**
whyNot.C: **Normal resting wall motion**; the defect is regional and appears only with stress
whyNot.D: **No murmur**
whyNot.E: **Clear chest** and a regional wall-motion defect with stress

why: **Regional stress-induced wall-motion defect in a smoker with a family history of early MI** = flow-limiting coronary atherosclerosis.

stem: A 63-year-old man with diabetes has exertional chest pressure. At angiography, the vessels show diffuse irregular luminal narrowing. Intracoronary acetylcholine makes the diseased segments narrow, while nitroglycerin dilates them. He has no cocaine use, no atrial arrhythmia, and no recent emotional stress.
oneliner: 63M + diabetes + exertional chest pressure + diffuse irregular coronary narrowing + paradoxical constriction with acetylcholine → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Diffuse fixed narrowing with exertional pain**; Prinzmetal is rest pain with ST elevation in otherwise smooth vessels
whyNot.B: **No cocaine use**
whyNot.D: **No emotional stressor**, and exertional pain with diffuse luminal disease
whyNot.E: **No atrial arrhythmia** and diffuse rather than abrupt single-vessel cutoff

why: **Diffuse luminal irregularity + constriction to acetylcholine** = atherosclerosis with loss of endothelial nitric oxide.

stem: A 62-year-old man with exertional chest pain develops ST depression in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6 on exercise testing. Angiography shows 85% stenosis of a vessel running in the left atrioventricular groove.
oneliner: 62M + exertional chest pain + exercise ST depression I, aVL, V5–V6 + 85% stenosis in left AV groove vessel → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Lateral rather than anterior leads (V1–V4)**; the LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove
whyNot.B: **Lateral rather than inferior leads (II, III, aVF)**
whyNot.C: **Exertional pain with ST depression**, not rest pain with ST elevation
whyNot.E: **Exertional pain, ST depression, and a focal vessel stenosis**

why: **Lateral-lead ischemia + stenosis in the left AV groove** = left circumflex artery supplying the lateral left ventricle.

stem: A 58-year-old man has had substernal pressure each time he climbs two flights of stairs for the past 8 months. It lasts about 5 minutes and stops when he rests. The pattern has not changed. Resting ECG is normal and exercise testing reproduces the pain with ST depression.
oneliner: 58M + substernal pressure on 2 flights of stairs ×8 months + gone in 5 min with rest + unchanged pattern + exercise ST depression → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Exertional pain with ST depression**, not rest pain with ST elevation
whyNot.B: **Unchanged, predictable pattern**; unstable angina is new, worsening, or at rest
whyNot.C: **Exertional trigger and ST depression**, not pleuritic pain with diffuse ST elevation
whyNot.D: **5-minute pain relieved by rest** and a normal resting ECG

why: **Predictable exertional pain relieved by rest with ischemic ST depression** = fixed coronary stenosis (stable angina).

stem: A 69-year-old man has 30 minutes of chest pressure at rest, his third episode this week, each at lower exertion. ECG shows T-wave inversion in V2–V5 without ST elevation. Troponin is normal on two measurements 6 hours apart.
oneliner: 69M + rest chest pressure 30 min, 3rd episode this week + T inversion V2–V5 + normal troponin ×2 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal troponin**
whyNot.C: **Rest pain with increasing frequency**
whyNot.D: **Regional T inversion without diffuse ST elevation or PR depression**
whyNot.E: **No ST elevation**

why: **New rest pain with T-wave inversion and normal troponin** = ischemia without necrosis (unstable angina).

stem: A 60-year-old man had a bare-metal stent placed in the left anterior descending artery 4 months ago and was symptom-free after. Over the past 3 weeks he has had gradually increasing chest pain on exertion that eases with rest. ECG at rest is normal and troponin is normal.
oneliner: 60M + bare-metal stent to LAD 4 months ago + symptom-free + 3 weeks of gradual exertional angina + normal troponin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Gradual onset months later**; stent thrombosis is abrupt with infarction, usually in the first weeks
whyNot.C: **Exertional, not rest, pain** at the stented site
whyNot.D: **Dissection occurs at the time of the procedure**, not months later
whyNot.E: **Gradually worsening exertional ischemia**, not an acute event or incidental dilation

why: **Gradual recurrence of exertional angina 3–6 months after stenting** = smooth muscle proliferation narrowing the stent.

stem: A 66-year-old man has 90 minutes of substernal chest pain with sweating. Pulse is 108/min, BP is 100/70 mm Hg and equal in both arms, and respirations are 22/min. His jugular veins are distended and he has bibasilar crackles. ECG shows ST elevation in V4–V6 and new Q waves in the same leads.
oneliner: 66M + substernal pain 90 min + sweating + JVD + basal crackles + ST elevation V4–V6 + new Q waves → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **ST elevation limited to V4–V6 with Q waves**; pericarditis is diffuse with PR depression
whyNot.C: **Equal arm pressures** and regional ST elevation with Q waves
whyNot.D: **Regional ST elevation with Q waves and basal crackles**, not a clear chest with sinus tachycardia
whyNot.E: **ST elevation with new Q waves** indicates transmural infarction

answer: Anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction (with left heart failure)
why: **Regional ST elevation V4–V6 + new Q waves + chest pain** = anterolateral STEMI; JVD and crackles show pump failure.

stem: A 61-year-old man has 1 hour of crushing chest pain. ECG shows ST elevation in V1–V4. On examination there is an S4 and a soft apical systolic murmur. BP is equal in both arms and the chest x-ray shows a normal mediastinum.
oneliner: 61M + 1 h crushing chest pain + ST elevation V1–V4 + S4 + soft apical systolic murmur + normal mediastinum → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Equal arm pressures and normal mediastinum**
whyNot.C: **Regional ST elevation with an S4**; no friction rub or diffuse change
whyNot.D: **ST elevation** indicates transmural infarction
whyNot.E: **ST elevation V1–V4 with an S4 and apical murmur**, not isolated tachycardia and hypoxia

why: **Crushing pain + ST elevation V1–V4** = anterior STEMI; the S4 and apical murmur reflect a stiff ischemic ventricle and papillary muscle dysfunction.

stem: A 65-year-old man, two days after admission for chest pain, has light-headedness and a pulse of 44/min. ECG shows progressive PR lengthening before each dropped QRS. His admission ECG showed ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF.
oneliner: 65M + 2 d after chest pain + pulse 44 + progressive PR lengthening with dropped beats + admission ST elevation II, III, aVF → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Inferior-lead ST elevation**, not V1–V4
whyNot.B: **Inferior rather than I, aVL, V5–V6 elevation**
whyNot.C: **ST elevation in inferior leads**, not ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3
whyNot.E: **Elevation limited to inferior leads with AV block**; pericarditis is diffuse

why: **ST elevation in II, III, aVF + AV block** = inferior MI, where the occluded artery also supplies the AV node.

stem: A 62-year-old man with an inferior STEMI still has chest pain after sublingual nitroglycerin and is given IV morphine. Within minutes his face is flushed and his chest itches. BP falls from 118/76 to 92/58 mm Hg and pulse is 96/min. He has no wheeze, no lip swelling, clear lungs, and flat neck veins.
oneliner: 62M + inferior STEMI + IV morphine → flushing + itching + BP 118/76 → 92/58 + clear lungs, flat neck veins, no wheeze → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his new symptoms?

whyNot.A: **No wheeze or lip swelling**
whyNot.B: **Flat neck veins and clear lungs** with flushing and itching
whyNot.C: **Flat neck veins**; RV infarct causes distended veins with clear lungs
whyNot.D: **Flat neck veins** and no muffled heart sounds

why: **Flushing and itching minutes after IV morphine** = direct mast cell histamine release causing vasodilation and hypotension.

dx: Right heart failure after right ventricular infarction
stem: A 66-year-old man had an inferior MI with right ventricular involvement 6 weeks ago. He now has abdominal swelling, tender liver enlargement, ascites, raised jugular venous pressure, and ankle edema. His lungs are clear, there is no pericardial knock, urinalysis shows no protein, and he has no spider angiomata.
oneliner: 66M + RV infarct 6 weeks ago + abdominal swelling + tender hepatomegaly + ascites + raised JVP + ankle edema + clear lungs + no pericardial knock → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Raised JVP and a tender, congested liver with no spider angiomata**
whyNot.B: **No pericardial knock and a clear prior RV infarct** to explain the venous congestion
whyNot.D: **No proteinuria**
whyNot.E: **Clear lungs**; left failure causes pulmonary congestion

why: **RV infarct + raised JVP + congested liver and ascites with clear lungs** = right-sided failure with systemic venous congestion.

stem: A 63-year-old man with 2 years of exertional chest pain wakes with severe crushing pain and sweating that lasts 10 hours and is not eased by rest. Pulse is 105/min. The pain does not change with breathing or position, and BP is equal in both arms with a normal mediastinum on chest x-ray. CK-MB is 62 ng/mL (normal <5).
oneliner: 63M + known exertional angina + severe pain 10 h at rest + sweating + CK-MB 62 + equal arm BPs, normal mediastinum → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Raised CK-MB** shows myocardial necrosis
whyNot.C: **Equal arm pressures and normal mediastinum**
whyNot.D: **Pain unchanged by breathing or position**
whyNot.E: **10-hour rest pain with raised CK-MB**, not brief exertional pain

why: **Prolonged rest pain with diaphoresis and raised CK-MB** = myocardial necrosis, not angina.

stem: Ten minutes after a coronary artery is ligated in a rat, electron microscopy of the ischemic myocytes shows swollen cells and mitochondria, plasma membrane blebs, and ribosomes detached from the endoplasmic reticulum. The nuclei and membranes are intact.
oneliner: Rat + coronary ligation 10 min + EM: swollen cells and mitochondria, membrane blebs, ribosomes detached from ER, intact nuclei → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Nuclei intact and no amorphous mitochondrial densities or membrane defects**
whyNot.B: **Too early (needs hours) and nuclei are still intact**
whyNot.C: **The ligation is still in place**, with no restored flow
whyNot.D: **Cells are swollen**, not shrunken with condensed chromatin

why: **Early ischemia with cell and mitochondrial swelling, blebs, and intact nuclei** = reversible injury from ATP depletion and sodium-pump failure.

stem: A 55-year-old man with asthma and nasal polyps is discharged one week after an MI. An hour after his first dose of aspirin he develops wheezing and a runny nose. He has no hives, no lip swelling, and a BP of 124/80 mm Hg. His neck veins are flat and his lungs have no crackles.
oneliner: 55M + asthma + nasal polyps + 1 wk post-MI + wheeze and rhinorrhea 1 h after aspirin + no hives, flat neck veins, no crackles → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No hives or lip swelling and normal BP**
whyNot.B: **Acute reaction timed to the first aspirin dose**; EGPA is a chronic eosinophilic vasculitis, not a drug-triggered attack
whyNot.C: **Flat neck veins and no crackles**
whyNot.E: **Reaction timed to aspirin intake**, not recurrent infiltrates

why: **Asthma + nasal polyps + wheeze after aspirin** = COX-1 inhibition shifts arachidonic acid toward leukotrienes.

stem: A 67-year-old man with severe three-vessel coronary disease had an episode of prolonged chest pain 3 weeks ago. He dies suddenly of ventricular fibrillation. At autopsy the anterolateral left ventricular wall has a depressed red-gray area. A microscopic section of this area is shown.
oneliner: 67M + chest pain 3 wk ago + sudden death + depressed red-gray anterolateral area + [histology] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No neutrophil-rich coagulative necrosis**; the section shows repair tissue
whyNot.B: **Not near-normal tissue with wavy fibers**
whyNot.C: **Not a dense, relatively acellular collagen scar**
whyNot.E: **Repair tissue limited to one territory, not diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate**

why: **Loose vascular granulation tissue replacing necrotic myocytes** about 2–3 weeks after an infarct.

image.prompt: H&E-stained section of heart muscle in which most myocytes are gone, replaced by loose pink connective tissue full of new thin-walled capillaries, plump fibroblasts, and scattered macrophages, with a few leftover pale necrotic muscle fibers at the edge. No dense scar and no sheets of neutrophils.

stem: A 70-year-old man dies of cardiogenic shock 5 days after a massive anterior MI. At autopsy the infarcted wall is yellow-tan and soft. Microscopy shows dead myocytes without nuclei, disintegrating neutrophils, and many macrophages clearing the debris, and no collagen or new vessels.
oneliner: 70M + died day 5 after massive anterior MI + yellow-tan soft wall + dead myocytes + fading neutrophils + many macrophages, no collagen → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Dead myocytes with an inflammatory infiltrate**, not near-normal fibers
whyNot.B: **No granulation tissue, collagen, or new vessels**
whyNot.D: **No collagen scar**
whyNot.E: **Neutrophils and necrosis in one territory**, not diffuse lymphocytes

why: **Coagulative necrosis with macrophages replacing neutrophils and no repair tissue** = day 3–7 of infarction; cardiac myocytes are permanent cells, so the area heals by scar.

stem: A 64-year-old woman has sudden severe dyspnea 2 days after an inferior MI. BP is 84/50 mm Hg and she has bilateral crackles. There is a new loud holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, with no thrill at the left sternal border. Her neck veins are distended but heart sounds are not muffled.
oneliner: 64F + 2 d post inferior MI + sudden dyspnea + crackles + new loud apical holosystolic murmur to axilla + no thrill, not muffled → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla**, not at the left lower sternal border with a thrill
whyNot.C: **Loud murmur and pulmonary edema**; tamponade gives muffled sounds
whyNot.D: **Loud holosystolic murmur**, not a friction rub
whyNot.E: **Too early (weeks) and acute pulmonary edema**

why: **Day 2 post-MI, acute pulmonary edema, and a new apical holosystolic murmur to the axilla** = ruptured papillary muscle.

stem: A 58-year-old man with an anterior STEMI has a stent placed, restoring full flow. Two hours later the ST elevation has resolved, but CK-MB rises from 80 to 310 ng/mL. Repeat angiography shows a widely patent stent with no clot.
oneliner: 58M + anterior STEMI + stent with full flow + ST resolved but CK-MB 80 → 310 + repeat angiogram: patent stent, no clot → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Ongoing myocardial infarction from persistent occlusion

whyNot.A: **Patent stent and resolved ST elevation**
whyNot.B: **Patent stent with no clot**
whyNot.C: **Marked enzyme rise**, which indicates cell death rather than reversible dysfunction
whyNot.D: **Acute rise in enzymes after reopening**, not chronic low flow

why: **Enzyme rise after flow is restored through a patent stent** = oxygen free radical damage on reperfusion.

stem: A rat heart is perfused with oxygenated buffer after 30 minutes of global ischemia. Myocytes then show hypercontraction bands and swollen mitochondria. The damage is reduced when superoxide dismutase and catalase are added.
oneliner: Rat heart + 30 min ischemia then oxygenated reperfusion + contraction bands + swollen mitochondria + prevented by SOD and catalase → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Damage appears after restored flow and is rescued by free radical scavengers**
whyNot.C: **Structural myocyte damage**, not just reversible contractile dysfunction
whyNot.D: **Contraction bands and swelling**, not shrinkage with chromatin condensation
whyNot.E: **Acute flow restoration** with oxidative injury rather than chronic low flow

why: **Damage that worsens after flow returns and is blocked by superoxide scavengers** = oxygen free radical reperfusion injury.

stem: A 24-year-old man has an LDL of 260 mg/dL with normal triglycerides and bilateral Achilles tendon xanthomas.
oneliner: 24M + LDL 260 + normal triglycerides + Achilles tendon xanthomas → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal triglycerides**
whyNot.B: **High LDL with normal triglycerides**
whyNot.D: **High LDL**; LDL is nearly absent in this condition
whyNot.E: **Normal triglycerides**; chylomicronemia would give very high levels

why: **Very high LDL with tendon xanthomas in a young man and normal triglycerides** = defective LDL receptor.

stem: A 52-year-old overweight man (BMI 29 kg/m²) with hypertension has a fasting lipid panel: total cholesterol 240 mg/dL, LDL 170 mg/dL, HDL 35 mg/dL, triglycerides 175 mg/dL. He has no xanthomas, and his TSH is normal.
oneliner: 52M + BMI 29 + hypertension + TC 240 + LDL 170 + HDL 35 + TG 175 + no xanthomas → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Low HDL and raised triglycerides with no xanthomas**; LDL only 170
whyNot.B: **LDL is high** and triglycerides only 175
whyNot.D: **Lipids are raised**, not nearly absent
whyNot.E: **HDL is 35, not near zero**, with no orange tonsils

answer: Mixed dyslipidemia (high LDL, borderline high triglycerides, low HDL)
why: **Raised LDL + low HDL + mildly raised triglycerides** in an overweight hypertensive man = mixed dyslipidemia.

stem: A 45-year-old man has a fasting triglyceride level of 550 mg/dL with an LDL of 95 mg/dL, and diet changes have not helped. He has no history of pancreatitis, and his plasma is cloudy but not milky.
oneliner: 45M + fasting TG 550 + LDL 95 + diet failed + no pancreatitis + cloudy plasma → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal LDL**
whyNot.B: **Normal LDL with only triglycerides raised**; dysbetalipoproteinemia raises cholesterol and triglycerides together
whyNot.C: **Plasma not milky, TG well below 1,000, and no pancreatitis**
whyNot.E: **Raised triglycerides**; lipids are very low in this condition

why: **Isolated triglyceride elevation with normal LDL** = hypertriglyceridemia.

stem: A 40-year-old man has fasting LDL 190 mg/dL and triglycerides 350 mg/dL, with HDL 35 mg/dL. His father had an MI at age 48 and his brother has high triglycerides alone. He has no xanthomas and a normal TSH.
oneliner: 40M + LDL 190 + TG 350 + HDL 35 + father MI at 48 + brother with high TG only + no xanthomas, normal TSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Raised triglycerides and no xanthomas**
whyNot.B: **LDL is also raised**
whyNot.D: **No palmar xanthomas** and the LDL is raised
whyNot.E: **Normal TSH**

why: **Raised LDL and triglycerides with a family history of premature CAD and varying patterns in relatives** = familial combined hyperlipidemia.

stem: A 62-year-old man with diabetes and a 40 pack-year smoking history has calf pain after walking two blocks that stops within 3 minutes of standing still. Femoral pulses are normal, pedal pulses are weak, and the ankle-brachial index is 0.67. His legs are not swollen and he has no back pain.
oneliner: 62M + diabetes + 40 pack-years + calf pain after 2 blocks relieved by standing rest + weak pedal pulses + ABI 0.67 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Weak pedal pulses and low ABI, with no back pain**
whyNot.B: **No leg swelling** and pain is exertional
whyNot.C: **Pain brought on by walking and relieved by rest** with a low ABI
whyNot.D: **No leg swelling**, exertional pain, and a low ABI

why: **Exertional calf pain relieved by rest + weak pulses + ABI 0.67** = atherosclerotic limb ischemia.

stem: A 66-year-old man with 20 years of hypertension has had a week of worsening breathlessness on exertion and now sleeps on three pillows, waking at night short of breath. He has raised jugular venous pressure, an S3, bibasilar crackles, and pitting ankle edema. Chest x-ray shows an enlarged heart with upper-lobe vascular congestion.
oneliner: 66M + hypertension 20 yr + exertional dyspnea + 3 pillows + PND + raised JVP + S3 + crackles + edema + cardiomegaly on CXR → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

whyNot.B: **S3, crackles, and upper-lobe congestion with a large heart**; tamponade gives clear lungs and muffled sounds
whyNot.C: **Orthopnea, PND, crackles, and a large heart after long-standing hypertension** point to the left heart
whyNot.D: **Enlarged heart and an S3**, not a small calcified heart with a pericardial knock
whyNot.E: **S3, raised JVP, edema, and cardiomegaly** point to a cardiac cause

why: **Orthopnea + PND + raised JVP + S3 + crackles + cardiomegaly** after long-standing hypertension = congestive heart failure.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with coronary disease has had 12 hours of worsening breathlessness. Respirations are 30/min, oxygen saturation is 86% on room air, and temperature is 37.0°C. She has bilateral rales to the mid-lung fields, an S3 gallop, and raised jugular venous pressure. There is no wheeze and her legs are not swollen or tender.
oneliner: 72F + CAD + 12 h worsening dyspnea + RR 30 + SpO2 86% + afebrile + bilateral rales + S3 + raised JVP + no wheeze → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Afebrile with bilateral rales, an S3, and raised JVP**
whyNot.B: **S3, raised JVP, and diffuse rales**; PE typically has clear lungs
whyNot.C: **S3 and raised JVP** point to a cardiac cause
whyNot.D: **No wheeze**

answer: Acute decompensated heart failure (cardiogenic pulmonary edema)
why: **Rapid dyspnea with S3, raised JVP, rales, and hypoxemia** = pulmonary edema from decompensated heart failure.

stem: A 64-year-old man has two-pillow orthopnea and leg edema that began 5 days after an episode of 40 minutes of chest pain he did not report. He has an S3, a regular pulse of 78/min, and no murmur.
oneliner: 64M + orthopnea + leg edema + began 5 d after 40 min of chest pain + S3 + regular pulse 78 + no murmur → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No murmur**
whyNot.B: **No murmur**; AR gives an early diastolic murmur
whyNot.D: **Orthopnea, S3, and bilateral edema** after chest pain, not pleuritic pain and tachycardia
whyNot.E: **Regular pulse of 78/min**, not a slow dissociated rhythm

why: **Orthopnea + edema + S3 following a silent infarct** = ischemic left ventricular dysfunction.

stem: A 70-year-old man had an MI 6 months ago. He now has distended neck veins, bibasilar crackles, and pitting edema. Serum sodium is 129 mEq/L, BUN is 30 mg/dL, creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL, and urine sodium is 8 mEq/L (low).
oneliner: 70M + MI 6 mo ago + JVD + crackles + pitting edema + Na 129 + low urine Na 8 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Edema, JVD, and low urine sodium**; SIADH is euvolemic with urine sodium above 40
whyNot.C: **Raised neck veins and lung crackles after an MI** point to the heart; nephrotic edema does not raise the JVP
whyNot.D: **Raised neck veins and lung crackles after an MI**; cirrhosis does not raise the JVP
whyNot.E: **Creatinine 1.3 with low urine sodium** from reduced perfusion, not renal injury

why: **Prior MI + JVD, crackles, edema + low urine sodium** = failing heart with effective arterial underfilling and ADH release.

dx: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
stem: A 71-year-old woman with 20 years of untreated hypertension takes ibuprofen daily. She has had 2 weeks of breathlessness and ankle swelling. BP is 168/98 mm Hg. She has an S4, raised jugular venous pressure, bibasilar crackles, and no murmur. Echo shows symmetric concentric wall thickening and an ejection fraction of 62%.
oneliner: 71F + untreated hypertension 20 yr + daily NSAID + dyspnea + edema + S4 + raised JVP + crackles + no murmur + concentric LVH, EF 62% → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

whyNot.A: **No murmur**
whyNot.C: **Crackles with a thick left ventricle** point to the left heart, not primary right-sided failure
whyNot.D: **Symmetric, not asymmetric septal, thickening** with long-standing hypertension
whyNot.E: **Preserved ejection fraction** with a thick, not dilated, ventricle

answer: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (diastolic heart failure)
why: **Long-standing hypertension + S4 + congestion + EF 62% with concentric LVH** = diastolic dysfunction.

stem: A 68-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 25% takes lisinopril and furosemide. He has persistent leg edema, distended neck veins, an S3, and bibasilar crackles. Serum potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. His urinalysis shows no protein and he has no ascites or spider angiomata.
oneliner: 68M + EF 25% on lisinopril + furosemide + persistent edema + JVD + S3 + crackles + K 3.1 + no proteinuria, no ascites → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No proteinuria**
whyNot.C: **Dilated, poorly contracting ventricle (EF 25%) and an S3**
whyNot.D: **EF 25% with crackles** points to left ventricular failure, not primary right-sided failure
whyNot.E: **Raised neck veins, S3, and EF of 25%**, with no ascites or spider angiomata

why: **EF 25% + JVD, S3, crackles, and edema despite loop diuretic** = congestive failure; the low potassium reflects diuretic loss.

stem: A 60-year-old man has exertional dyspnea and cool extremities. Hemodynamics: cardiac output 3.1 L/min (normal 4–8), central venous pressure 14 mm Hg (normal 2–8), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 26 mm Hg (normal 6–12), left ventricular ejection fraction 22%, systemic vascular resistance 1,800 dyne·s/cm⁵ (normal 800–1,200).
oneliner: 60M + exertional dyspnea + cool extremities + CO 3.1 + CVP 14 + wedge 26 + EF 22% + SVR 1,800 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

whyNot.B: **Raised wedge pressure**, which is normal in pure right-sided failure
whyNot.C: **EF 22%**; restrictive disease preserves ejection fraction
whyNot.D: **Low cardiac output and high resistance**; shunts give high output and low resistance
whyNot.E: **Wedge pressure far above CVP**; tamponade equalizes the pressures

answer: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
why: **Low CO + low EF + high wedge pressure + high SVR** = depressed contractility with raised filling pressures.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with chronic congestive heart failure dies of respiratory failure. At autopsy her lungs are heavy and congested. A section of her kidney cortex is shown.
oneliner: 78F + chronic congestive heart failure + heavy congested lungs at autopsy + [kidney histology] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Nuclei are preserved, tubules are intact, and there are no sloughed cells or casts**
whyNot.C: **Cytoplasm is clear from water**, not discrete lipid vacuoles
whyNot.D: **Swollen cells**, not single shrunken cells with fragmented nuclei
whyNot.E: **Cells are swollen with nuclei still present**, not shrunken, eosinophilic ghosts

answer: Reversible cell injury (hydropic change from chronic hypoxia)
why: **Swollen tubular cells with pale cytoplasm and preserved nuclei** in chronic heart failure = reversible hypoxic injury from failed sodium-potassium pumps.

image.prompt: H&E-stained section of kidney cortex in which proximal tubular epithelial cells are enlarged with pale, clear, finely vacuolated cytoplasm that narrows the tubule lumens. Nuclei are present and stain normally, and tubular outlines and glomeruli are intact.

stem: A 54-year-old man was stabbed below the left clavicle 15 years ago. He now has progressive dyspnea and leg edema. BP is 130/50 mm Hg, pulse is 98/min, and his extremities are warm with bounding pulses. A thrill and continuous machine-like murmur are felt over the left infraclavicular area.
oneliner: 54M + stab wound under left clavicle 15 yr ago + dyspnea + edema + BP 130/50 + warm bounding pulses + continuous murmur and thrill there → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Warm extremities, wide pulse pressure, and a continuous murmur** point to excess flow, not a weak pump
whyNot.C: **Wide pulse pressure and a continuous infraclavicular murmur** point to a shunt, not pulmonary hypertension
whyNot.D: **Warm skin, bounding pulses, and a wide pulse pressure**; constriction gives a low-output state
whyNot.E: **Murmur is continuous over the clavicle**, not diastolic at the left sternal border

why: **Old penetrating injury + continuous murmur + warm skin and wide pulse pressure** = AV fistula shunting blood and overloading the heart.

stem: A 44-year-old man has had 3 months of cough and breathlessness on exertion. He has bibasilar crackles and an S3 but no murmur. Echo shows a dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesis and an ejection fraction of 20%. The valves and wall thickness are normal and there is no pericardial fluid.
oneliner: 44M + 3 months of cough and exertional dyspnea + crackles + S3 + no murmur + dilated LV, global hypokinesis, EF 20% → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Dilated, not thickened, ventricle**
whyNot.B: **No pericardial fluid on echo**
whyNot.C: **Dilated LV with low EF and normal wall thickness**
whyNot.D: **Normal valves and no murmur**

why: **Dilated LV with global hypokinesis, low EF, and normal valves** = dilated cardiomyopathy with systolic failure.

stem: A 58-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure has difficulty swallowing solids but not liquids. A barium esophagram is shown.
oneliner: 58M + dilated cardiomyopathy + dysphagia for solids, not liquids + [barium swallow] → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause of the dysphagia?

whyNot.A: **Smooth extrinsic indentation, not an irregular mucosal narrowing**
whyNot.C: **Esophagus is not dilated with a tapered bird-beak end**
whyNot.D: **Displacement at the level of the heart**, not the aortic knob
whyNot.E: **No pouch** at the upper esophagus

answer: Enlarged left atrium compressing the esophagus
why: **Smooth posterior indentation of the mid-esophagus behind the heart** = extrinsic compression by an enlarged left atrium.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has a cough, difficulty breathing when lying flat, and leg swelling 1 month after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. She is afebrile, her BP is 118/76 mm Hg, her legs are not tender, and urinalysis is normal. She has raised jugular venous pressure, an S3, and bibasilar crackles.
oneliner: 31F + 1 month postpartum + cough + orthopnea + leg swelling + afebrile + normal BP and urinalysis + raised JVP + S3 + crackles → ?

whyNot.E: **Normal BP and urinalysis**

stem: A 27-year-old woman had fever, sore throat, and muscle aches 2 weeks ago, which have resolved. She now has breathlessness on exertion and cannot lie flat. Pulse is 112/min and BP is 100/66 mm Hg. She has an S3 and bibasilar crackles, with no murmur, joint pain, chest pain, or friction rub. Echo shows a dilated, globally hypokinetic left ventricle. oneliner: 27F + viral illness 2 wk ago + exertional dyspnea + orthopnea + S3 + crackles + dilated hypokinetic LV + biopsy: lymphocytes with myocyte necrosis → ?

stem: A 19-year-old male basketball player faints during a game. He has a systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that gets softer when he lies down and raises his legs.
oneliner: 19M + basketball player + syncope during game + systolic murmur that softens with leg raise → ?

stem: A 24-year-old sedentary man has exertional light-headedness and palpitations. His apex beat is forceful and sustained. BP is 118/72 mm Hg. Echo shows an interventricular septum of 2.4 cm (normal 0.6–1.1) and a posterior wall of 1.0 cm, with a small ventricular cavity and a normal aortic valve.

stem: A 66-year-old man with multiple myeloma (IgG kappa spike and lytic bone lesions) has breathlessness and leg swelling. Echo shows a thick, echodense left ventricle with a normal ejection fraction, poor diastolic filling, and small pleural and pericardial effusions. A Congo red-stained section of an endomyocardial biopsy viewed under polarized light is shown.

ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Deposits stain with Congo red rather than showing sheets of plasma cells**
whyNot.B: **Biopsy shows extracellular deposits, not myocyte disarray**
whyNot.D: **No inflammatory infiltrate**; there are extracellular deposits

stem: A 68-year-old man faints while climbing stairs. He has a harsh late-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to the neck, and a small, slow-rising carotid pulse.
oneliner: 68M + syncope on exertion + harsh late-peaking systolic murmur at right upper sternal border to neck + small slow-rising carotid pulse → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Slow-rising small carotid pulse**; HCM gives a brisk upstroke
whyNot.B: **Ejection murmur radiating to the neck**, not a midsystolic click with a late murmur
whyNot.C: **Murmur at the right upper sternal border**, not a holosystolic apical murmur
whyNot.E: **Exertional syncope with an ejection murmur and slow-rising pulse**; dissection presents with sudden tearing pain

why: **Exertional syncope + late-peaking ejection murmur to the carotids + pulsus parvus et tardus** = fixed outflow obstruction at the aortic valve.

stem: An 84-year-old woman has breathlessness on walking. She has a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to the neck. Echo shows a heavily calcified, thickened tricuspid aortic valve with restricted leaflet opening.
oneliner: 84F + exertional dyspnea + crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at RUSB to neck + heavily calcified, restricted aortic valve on echo → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the neck**, not a holosystolic apical murmur
whyNot.B: **Crescendo-decrescendo murmur with a calcified aortic valve**, not a click
whyNot.C: **Systolic ejection murmur**, not a decrescendo diastolic murmur
whyNot.E: **Systolic murmur** and no diastolic rumble

why: **Crescendo-decrescendo murmur to the neck + calcified, restricted valve in a very old patient** = degenerative calcific aortic stenosis.

stem: An 81-year-old man has exertional dyspnea and light-headedness. A very soft ejection murmur is barely heard. His pulses are small and slow to rise and the second heart sound is single. Echo shows a heavily calcified, nearly immobile aortic valve and an ejection fraction of 25%.
oneliner: 81M + exertional dyspnea + light-headedness + barely audible soft ejection murmur + small slow pulses + single S2 + immobile calcified aortic valve, EF 25% → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Calcified immobile aortic valve** and slow-rising pulses
whyNot.B: **Heavily calcified aortic valve** with a single S2
whyNot.D: **No holosystolic apical murmur**
whyNot.E: **Calcified, immobile aortic valve** on echo and slow-rising pulses

why: **Immobile calcified valve + slow-rising pulses + single S2** = severe aortic stenosis; a failing ventricle lowers flow and softens the murmur.

stem: A 70-year-old man has exertional chest pain and a systolic thrill at the right upper sternal border with a crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the neck. Cardiac catheterization: left ventricular pressure 230/25 mm Hg, aortic pressure 140/80 mm Hg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 22 mm Hg (normal 6–12).
oneliner: 70M + exertional chest pain + systolic thrill RUSB + murmur to neck + LV 230/25 vs aorta 140/80 + wedge 22 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **LV systolic pressure 90 mm Hg above the aorta**, a gradient MR does not cause
whyNot.C: **Normal aortic pulse pressure (60) and a systolic, not diastolic, murmur**
whyNot.D: **Large pressure gradient** across the aortic valve
whyNot.E: **Thrill and murmur at the aortic area, radiating to the neck**, with a fixed valve-level gradient

why: **Systolic LV-to-aorta gradient of 90 mm Hg with a thrill and murmur to the neck** = valvular outflow obstruction.

stem: A 69-year-old man has exertional chest pain. Coronary angiography shows no stenosis. He has a harsh late-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to the carotids, and a soft A2.
oneliner: 69M + exertional chest pain + normal coronary angiogram + harsh late-peaking murmur RUSB to carotids + soft A2 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal coronary angiogram**
whyNot.B: **Late-peaking murmur with a soft A2 at the aortic area**
whyNot.D: **Exertional pain with a fixed murmur**, not rest pain
whyNot.E: **Exertional rather than tearing pain**, with a fixed ejection murmur

answer: Aortic stenosis (angina from increased oxygen demand)
why: **Angina with clean coronaries + late-peaking murmur to the carotids + soft A2** = aortic stenosis; the hypertrophied ventricle outstrips its supply.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border found at a routine visit. She has no symptoms, the murmur does not radiate, her carotid upstroke is normal, and S2 is normal. Echo shows thickened, calcified leaflets that open fully, with no pressure gradient.
oneliner: 72F + asymptomatic + grade 2/6 ejection murmur RUSB without radiation + normal carotid upstroke + normal S2 + calcified leaflets that open fully, no gradient → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No symptoms, normal carotid upstroke, and no gradient**
whyNot.B: **Calcified aortic leaflets and no septal thickening**
whyNot.C: **No chest pain or ischemic findings**; the murmur arises from the aortic valve
whyNot.D: **Murmur at the aortic area, ejection quality, and no apical holosystolic murmur**

why: **Soft ejection murmur with calcified leaflets that open fully and no gradient** = aortic sclerosis, without obstruction.

stem: A 47-year-old man collapses and dies while jogging. At autopsy, his aortic valve is examined. A photograph of the valve viewed from above is shown.
oneliner: 47M + collapses and dies while jogging + [gross photo of aortic valve] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No vegetations**
whyNot.C: **Two cusps with a raphe** (congenital shape), not three cusps fused at the commissures
whyNot.D: **Only two cusps**
whyNot.E: **Not redundant, floppy leaflets**; the valve is calcified

stem: A 58-year-old woman has 3 months of exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex and radiates to the axilla, and echocardiography shows an enlarged left atrium.
oneliner: 58F + exertional dyspnea + orthopnea + apical holosystolic murmur to axilla + big LA → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **diastolic** rumble with opening snap expected; this murmur is systolic
whyNot.C: **crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right upper sternal border** radiating to carotids; this one is at the apex to the axilla
whyNot.D: murmur is loudest at the **lower left sternal border**, not the apex
whyNot.E: **early diastolic decrescendo murmur** with wide pulse pressure; this murmur is systolic

why: **Apical holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla** with **left atrial enlargement** = mitral regurgitation (volume overload of LA).

stem: A 66-year-old man with childhood rheumatic fever is admitted with an acute inferior myocardial infarction. On day 4 he develops sudden pulmonary edema and a new loud apical systolic murmur. Left atrial pressure tracing shows tall v waves reaching 40 mm Hg (mean LA pressure 28 mm Hg); the aortic pressure tracing is normal with no diastolic drop.
oneliner: 66M + acute inferior MI + new apical systolic murmur + pulmonary edema + LA tracing with tall v waves → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: would give **diastolic** murmur and **low aortic diastolic pressure**; aortic tracing here is normal
whyNot.B: would show a **pressure gradient between LV and aorta**; no such gradient is described
whyNot.D: a late complication (weeks) with persistent ST elevation; **tall LA v waves** are not explained
whyNot.E: would show tall **a** waves and a **diastolic** LA-LV gradient; this is a systolic problem

answer: Mitral regurgitation (acute, papillary muscle dysfunction after MI)
why: **Tall v waves in the LA tracing** plus a **new systolic murmur after MI** = acute mitral regurgitation.

stem: A 31-year-old man who injects heroin has ascites and leg edema. His jugular venous pressure is raised with prominent v waves, a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border increases on inspiration, and the liver pulsates in systole.
oneliner: 31M + IV heroin + high JVP with v waves + systolic murmur LLSB louder on inspiration + pulsatile liver + ascites → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: murmur radiates to the axilla and does **not** get louder with inspiration; no pulsatile liver
whyNot.B: raised JVP and ascites but **no murmur**; a pericardial knock and Kussmaul sign instead of a pulsatile liver
whyNot.C: holosystolic murmur at the LLSB too, but it does **not increase with inspiration** and gives no **v waves or pulsatile liver**
whyNot.D: **crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border** with an ejection click, not a pansystolic LLSB murmur

why: **IV drug use**, **pulsatile liver**, **v waves** and an **inspiratory-augmented murmur at the LLSB** = tricuspid regurgitation (right-sided endocarditis).

stem: A 9-year-old boy has fever and painful swelling of the left knee, then the right ankle, then the elbow over 10 days; each joint settles in a few days. He had an untreated sore throat 3 weeks ago. There is a new apical murmur, blood cultures are negative, and the ASO titer is raised.
oneliner: 9M + sore throat 3 wk ago + migratory knee/ankle/elbow arthritis + new apical murmur + high ASO → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: persistent joint swelling over **6 weeks**, no strep trigger, no new murmur
whyNot.C: would have **positive blood cultures** and embolic signs; cultures are negative
whyNot.D: needs **conjunctivitis, red lips, rash**, typically under 5 years; arthritis is not migratory
whyNot.E: needs **tick exposure** and erythema migrans; **ASO is high** here

why: **Migratory polyarthritis**, **carditis** and **raised ASO** after untreated pharyngitis = acute rheumatic fever (Jones criteria).

stem: A 7-year-old girl has had fever and swelling of several joints that moved from one to another. She has a pink ring-shaped rash on the trunk, a markedly enlarged heart on chest x-ray, and a high anti-streptolysin O titer. She dies of heart failure; blood cultures were sterile.
oneliner: 7F + fever + migratory joint swelling + ring-shaped trunk rash + big heart + high ASO + fatal heart failure → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: blood cultures were **sterile**, and it does not give migratory arthritis with high ASO
whyNot.B: coronary aneurysms, **red lips and conjunctivae**; not a rising ASO with migratory arthritis
whyNot.C: no **migratory arthritis** or **marginate rash**, ASO not raised
whyNot.E: no **joint** involvement, no strep antibody response; chronic effusion rather than pancarditis

why: **Migratory arthritis**, **erythema marginatum** and **high ASO** with cardiomegaly = rheumatic fever with pancarditis.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with rheumatic fever in childhood has exertional dyspnea. A low-pitched diastolic rumble is heard at the apex. A lateral chest x-ray with barium swallow is shown.
oneliner: 38F + childhood rheumatic fever + exertional dyspnea + apical diastolic rumble + [lateral CXR with barium] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: murmur is **diastolic**, not holosystolic
whyNot.C: **early diastolic blowing murmur at the left sternal border** with wide pulse pressure; rumble here is at the apex
whyNot.D: follows MI and bulges the **left ventricle**, it does not push the esophagus back
whyNot.E: **systolic ejection murmur** to carotids; this murmur is diastolic

why: **Apical diastolic rumble**, rheumatic history and **backward displacement of the barium-filled esophagus** by a large left atrium = mitral stenosis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has progressive breathlessness when lying flat and rusty-coloured sputum. A low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble is heard at the apex. A photograph of her excised mitral valve is shown.
oneliner: 45F + orthopnea + rusty sputum + mid-diastolic apical murmur + [photo of valve] → ?

whyNot.A: floppy **billowing leaflets** with a mid-systolic click, not a diastolic murmur
whyNot.B: murmur is **diastolic**; valve would not be fused and narrowed
whyNot.C: an **aortic** valve disease with systolic murmur; this is the mitral valve

stem: A 34-year-old man with a known bicuspid aortic valve has had 3 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue and night sweats, starting a month after a dental extraction. A new diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border, and two blood culture sets grow gram-positive cocci in chains that are alpha-hemolytic.
oneliner: 34M + bicuspid aortic valve + dental extraction 1 mo ago + 3 wk low-grade fever + new diastolic murmur + blood cultures alpha-hemolytic strep → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: needs a **recent group A strep pharyngitis**, migratory arthritis and raised ASO; **cultures are positive** here
whyNot.C: bicuspid valve may stenose with age, but it does not cause **fever with bacteremia**
whyNot.D: **sterile** verrucae in lupus, so blood cultures would be negative
whyNot.E: gives fever and a diastolic murmur, but **cultures stay sterile** and the murmur changes with posture

why: **Abnormal valve**, **dental procedure** and **viridans streptococci in blood** = subacute infective endocarditis.

stem: A 27-year-old man who injects heroin has 5 days of fever and pleuritic chest pain. A new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border becomes louder on inspiration. He has no sinus symptoms and urinalysis is normal. A chest x-ray is shown.
oneliner: 27M + IV heroin + fever + pleuritic pain + new LLSB holosystolic murmur louder on inspiration + [CXR] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: chronic cough, weight loss and **upper-lobe** disease; it does not explain a **new tricuspid murmur**
whyNot.B: **lobar consolidation** with productive cough, not multiple cavitating nodules, and no murmur
whyNot.D: usually a **single** cavity after aspiration; here there are multiple nodules and a new murmur
whyNot.E: cavitating nodules, but would bring **sinus and kidney disease**, which are absent

answer: Infective endocarditis (right-sided, tricuspid, with septic pulmonary emboli)
why: **Injection drug use**, **new tricuspid murmur** and **multiple bilateral cavitating nodules** = tricuspid endocarditis with septic emboli.

image.prompt: Frontal chest x-ray showing multiple round nodules of varying size scattered in both lungs, several with thin-walled central cavities.

stem: A 2-year-old girl who is not cyanotic has poor weight gain, a soft systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and a wide, fixed split S2. ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy.
oneliner: 2F + poor weight gain + acyanotic + soft systolic murmur LUSB + wide fixed split S2 + RVH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border**, S2 splits normally with breathing
whyNot.B: **continuous machinery murmur** with bounding pulses
whyNot.D: **cyanosis** with a single S2; this child is not cyanotic
whyNot.E: **cyanosis and heart failure** early in infancy with a single S2

why: **Fixed wide splitting of S2** with a pulmonary flow murmur and right heart enlargement = atrial septal defect.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had several months of exertional dyspnea and tiredness. She looks well. There is a soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border and a wide S2 that does not change with breathing. ECG shows right axis deviation with incomplete right bundle branch block.
oneliner: 29F + months of exertional dyspnea + soft LUSB systolic murmur + fixed wide S2 + right axis deviation + incomplete RBBB → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border**; S2 not fixed
whyNot.B: **continuous machinery murmur** and bounding pulses
whyNot.C: **ejection click** and an S2 that varies with respiration
whyNot.D: **diastolic rumble** with an opening snap; this murmur is systolic and S2 is **fixed**

why: **Fixed split S2**, **right axis deviation and incomplete RBBB** = atrial septal defect.

stem: A 4-month-old boy who feeds and grows well has a harsh grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border. He is not cyanotic and femoral pulses are normal.
oneliner: 4M + thriving + harsh 4/6 holosystolic murmur at LLSB + acyanotic + normal femoral pulses → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **continuous machinery murmur** at the left upper sternal border
whyNot.C: **soft vibratory** grade 1-2 murmur; this one is loud and holosystolic
whyNot.D: would give **weak femoral pulses and arm-leg pressure difference**; femoral pulses are normal
whyNot.E: murmur is at the **apex radiating to the axilla**, rare in a thriving infant

why: **Harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border** in a well infant = ventricular septal defect.

stem: A 3-month-old girl breathes fast and tires during feeds. A holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border and she is not cyanotic. At cardiac catheterization, oxygen saturation is higher in the right ventricle than in the right atrium.
oneliner: 3F + tachypnea with feeds + holosystolic murmur + acyanotic + O2 step-up at the RV → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
